title: Number System and Number Properties
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Number System and Number Properties. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

coverage: Natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational and real numbers

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Learning route

Classify a number first, then use its properties to simplify a problem. The real number system contains rational and irrational numbers. Natural numbers are counting numbers; questions may specify whether zero is included. Whole numbers include zero; integers include negative whole numbers. A rational number is a quotient of integers with a nonzero denominator. Irrational numbers cannot be written as such a quotient.

Representation and structure

Rational decimals terminate or eventually repeat: (\(0.375=3/8\)) and (\(0.2727...=3/11\)). An irrational decimal neither terminates nor repeats. The square root of a nonnegative integer is rational exactly when the integer is a perfect square: (\(\sqrt{49}=7\)), while (\(\sqrt{3}\)) is irrational. Do not assume that every expression containing an irrational number is irrational: (\(\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}=2\)).

Integers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, but not division; (\(1/2\)) is not an integer. Rational numbers are closed under the four operations when division by zero is excluded. Real numbers are ordered on a number line, and infinitely many real numbers lie between any two distinct real numbers.

Parity, signs and factorisation

An even integer is divisible by 2; an odd integer leaves remainder 1 on division by 2. Even plus even and odd plus odd are even; even plus odd is odd. A product is even if at least one integer factor is even. Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, apart from factor order. One is neither prime nor composite.

Worked example: For odd (\(n\)), write (\(n=2k+1\)). Then (\(n(n+1)=(2k+1)(2k+2)=2(2k+1)(k+1)\)), so consecutive integers have an even product.

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
Choose a property before calculating

  • Use parity when only evenness or oddness is asked; full multiplication is unnecessary.
  • For a square-root classification, simplify the radicand to a perfect square times a square-free factor.
  • For a claim about every integer, use a symbolic form such as (\(n=2k\)) or (\(n=2k+1\)); examples alone do not prove a rule.
  • Check denominator restrictions before cancelling or dividing.

Frequent traps

  • Zero is even and an integer, but is not a positive natural number.
  • A prime has exactly two positive divisors; 1 has only one.
  • A rational plus an irrational is irrational, but two irrational numbers can have a rational sum.
  • Do not use real-number rules for square roots of negative values unless complex numbers are in scope.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Number sets: N is contained in Z, Z in Q, and Q in R; irrationals are R excluding Q.
  • Even: (\(2k\)). Odd: (\(2k+1\)), for integer k.
  • Prime factorisation: (\(N=p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...\)).
  • For nonzero a, (\(a^0=1\)); division by zero is undefined.
  • Rational decimal: terminating or recurring. Irrational decimal: nonterminating and nonrecurring.
  • Prove universal statements or disprove them with a valid counterexample.

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    If (\(n\)) is an odd integer, which expression is always even?

    1. (\(n^2\))
    2. (\(n^2+1\))
    3. (\(2n+1\))
    4. (\(n+2\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(n^2+1\))

    An odd square is odd. Adding 1 gives an even integer. The other three expressions are odd.

  2. Core:

    Which number is irrational?

    1. (\(\sqrt{49}\))
    2. (\(\frac{7}{11}\))
    3. (\(\sqrt{3}\))
    4. (\(0.125\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(\sqrt{3}\))

    (\(\sqrt{3}\)) is not a ratio of integers. The other values are rational: (\(7\)), (\(7/11\)), and (\(1/8\)).

  3. Foundation:

    For every integer (\(n\)), which product is always even?

    1. (\(n(n+1)\))
    2. (\(n^2+1\))
    3. (\(2n+1\))
    4. (\(n^2+n+1\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(n(n+1)\))

    One of two consecutive integers is even, so their product (\(n(n+1)\)) is even.

  4. Standard:

    Which expression is rational?

    1. (\(\sqrt{2}\))
    2. (\(\sqrt{18}/\sqrt{2}\))
    3. (pi)
    4. (\(\sqrt{5}+1\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(\sqrt{18}/\sqrt{2}\))

    (\(\sqrt{18}/\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{9}=3\)), which is rational. The other expressions are irrational.

  5. Challenge:

    If a is rational and b is irrational, which statement must be true?

    1. (\(a+b\)) is irrational
    2. (ab) is irrational for every a
    3. (\(a/b\)) is rational
    4. (b-a) is rational
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(a+b\)) is irrational

    A rational plus an irrational is irrational. The product claim fails for a=0; the quotient and difference are not generally rational.
